section_summary: This section documents political developments in Japan from late 1932 to April 1933, centering on the supremacy of the military clique over parliamentary government, the cabinet's preparations to withdraw from the League of Nations, and diplomatic tensions surrounding the invasion of Jehol. It includes diplomatic reports on the maneuvering of the Saito cabinet, the Seiyukai and Minseito parties, and Kenzo Adachi's fascist-leaning Kokumin Domei, alongside Diet debates challenging military dominance over foreign affairs. Additionally, the records detail a clandestine approach to the U.S. Consulate in Nagasaki by an agent of the secret direct-action society Ryodan, as well as high-level policy exchanges between Ambassador Grew, Secretary of State Stimson, and President Hoover concerning sanctions and the doctrine of non-recognition.

subfiles.about: Secretary of State Stimson commends Ambassador Grew's assessment of Japanese politics and his Osaka speech explaining American policy on peace treaties.
subfiles.summary: Stimson agrees with Grew's analysis of Japan's political situation, commending his Osaka speech explaining American peace-treaty support, closing with seasonal greetings.
subfiles.title: Letter from Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew regarding Political Situation in Japan

subfiles.about: A State Department cross-reference note referring to a memorandum by Maxwell M. Hamilton on the frequency of cabinet changes in Japan since May 1931.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Hamilton's 1932 memo counting Japanese government changes since May 1931, filed at 800.00/215.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet regarding Memorandum on Number of Changes of Government in Japan since May, 1931

subfiles.about: A State Department cross-reference note recording Secretary Stimson's observation that the Japanese government is entirely controlled by young army officers.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Stimson's 1933 memo: Tokyo's government had fallen entirely into young army officers' hands, eclipsing civilian authority.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet regarding Secretary of State's Memorandum on Military Control in Tokyo

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits reports from the Nagasaki Consulate detailing clandestine appeals by an agent of the secret direct-action society Ryodan seeking U.S. funds and assistance to overthrow Japan's military leaders.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew forwards correspondence and statements from Consul Henry B. Hitchcock and Vice Consul Glen Bruner in Nagasaki regarding nocturnal visits by Ippei Wada, who claimed to represent the anti-militarist patriotic society Ryodan. Wada requested 50,000 yen from the United States Government to procure explosives, offered to assist in smuggling munitions from American vessels, and claimed that the military clique under General Araki and General Minami fabricated the Mukden Incident and orchestrated political assassinations. Vice Consul Bruner and Consul Hitchcock firmly rebuffed Wada's requests, emphasizing that American authorities would have no connection with sedition or illegal plots, an attitude fully endorsed by Ambassador Grew and the State Department.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 233 enclosing Correspondence from Nagasaki regarding Ippei Wada and the Ryodan Secret Society

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports that the full text of Foreign Minister Uchida's foreign affairs address before the Diet is available at the Japanese Embassy in Washington.
subfiles.summary: Grew tells State that Foreign Minister Uchida's Diet address text is available via the Japanese Embassy, covering Manchuria, the League, and Soviet/U.S. relations.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 25 regarding Foreign Minister Uchida's Speech before the Diet

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet and accompanying excerpt from Tokyo's political report Despatch No. 245 analyzing budget controversies and military-party friction.
subfiles.summary: Despatch excerpt examines budget controversy over military spending, public/press opposition to military dictation, Seiyukai maneuvering, and Saito's threat of Diet dissolution leading to negotiated party support for the budget.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet with Extract from Despatch No. 245 regarding the Military Budget and Internal Politics

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum analyzing the founding, leadership, and fascist platform of Kenzo Adachi's newly formed political party, the Kokumin Domei.
subfiles.summary: Salisbury reviews Adachi's December 1932 founding of the Kokumin Domei from 33 mostly-Minseito Diet members, describing its fascist trappings and platform for state utility control and an Asiatic Monroe Doctrine, judging Adachi an opportunist unlikely to succeed.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on the Kokumin Domei, a New Political Party in Japan

subfiles.about: Communications between Ambassador Grew and the State Department confirming that telegrams from the Military Attaché in Tokyo to the War Department are shared with State.
subfiles.summary: Grew asks whether State receives Military Attaché telegrams; Salisbury confirms via Major Witsell, and Hornbeck's reply tells Grew such intelligence messages are indeed shared with the Department.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 40 with Memorandum and Reply regarding Military Attaché Telegrams from Tokyo

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew analyzes the political status of the Saito Cabinet, maneuvers among the Seiyukai, Minseito, and Kokumin Domei, and prospects for a successor government.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 266 presents an analysis of Japan's domestic political landscape, reporting that the emergency Saito super-party Cabinet is expected to resign following the close of the Diet session. The Seiyukai hopes to be asked by Prince Saionji to form a party cabinet, while the Minseito supports Saito to avoid an unconstrained Seiyukai administration, and Kenzo Adachi's Kokumin Domei attempts to exploit popular dissatisfaction. Grew observes that the public lacks confidence in traditional political parties and that interest in a fascist cabinet under Baron Hiranuma has declined, while emphasizing that no incoming cabinet is likely to alter Japan's defiant Manchurian policy.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 266 on the Political Situation in Japan

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on Lower House Diet interpellations by Dr. Hitoshi Ashida and Shinya Uchida challenging army dominance over diplomacy and military budgets.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports emerging parliamentary opposition to military dominance, highlighting interpellations in the Diet by Dr. Hitoshi Ashida, a Seiyukai member and publisher of the Japan Times and Mail. Ashida challenged War Minister Araki and Foreign Minister Uchida on whether the army was monopolizing policy in Manchuria and subjugating the Foreign Office. Grew also details criticisms of expanded army and navy budgets by Shinya Uchida, the evasive replies of government ministers, and encloses press clippings covering the debates, census statistics, and royal audiences for returning military commanders.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 271 regarding Opposition to the Military in the Diet

subfiles.about: A State Department charge slip recording the withdrawal or transfer of document 894.00/466.
subfiles.summary: Charge slip records file 894.00/466's checkout from the central decimal file, cross-referencing file 793.
subfiles.title: Charge Slip for File 894.00/466

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew delivers a grave appraisal of military supremacy in Japan, the decision to leave the League of Nations, the Jehol offensive, and risks of conflict with Western powers.
subfiles.summary: In Telegram No. 45, Ambassador Grew provides a comprehensive, strictly confidential estimate of conditions in Japan following the cabinet's decision to withdraw from the League of Nations, characterizing it as a complete triumph for the military. Grew describes the national psychology driving Japanese policy, including face-saving, belief in Manchuria as a vital lifeline, exasperation with China, and disregard for treaty obligations and financial costs. He warns that while Japan intends to avoid advancing south of the Great Wall into North China during the Jehol drive, active sanctions by the League would likely trigger the occupation of North China, while military propaganda has primed the public to accept eventual war with the United States or Russia as inevitable.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 45 regarding Far Eastern Situation, Withdrawal from the League, and Invasion of Jehol

subfiles.about: President Hoover responds to Ambassador Grew's dispatch, reaffirming his steadfast opposition to military or economic sanctions and advocating reliance solely on public opinion and non-recognition.
subfiles.summary: Hoover tells Stimson he firmly opposes sanctions against Japan, warning they'd escalate the crisis toward war, favoring moral pressure and non-recognition to mobilize opinion while allowing time for peaceful resolution.
subfiles.title: Letter from President Herbert Hoover to Secretary of State Stimson regarding Sanctions and Non-Recognition

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on the timetable for the Japanese army's offensive into Jehol and warns of potential direct action by the Young Officers Union against moderate statesmen.
subfiles.summary: Telegram relays that Japan's Jehol offensive starts imminently; the extremist Young Officers Union demanded League withdrawal, and radicals reportedly weighed violence against moderates like Shidehara, Makino, and Suzuki.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet and Telegram No. 44 on Jehol Offensive and Young Officers Union Threats

subfiles.about: Commercial Attaché Butts reports on domestic reactions to Dr. Ashida's Diet speech and quotes Yokohama Specie Bank President Kodama criticizing the Stimson doctrine.
subfiles.summary: Butts reports public reaction to Ashida's Diet speech questioning military dominance was limited to educated circles; banker Kodama said Stimson's policy would fail and U.S. concerns were fiscal, not political.
subfiles.title: Commercial Attaché Report Extract on Ashida's Speech and Yokohama Specie Bank Statements

subfiles.about: A State Department cross-reference note recording a public inquiry from Miss Ina Bowers requesting maps and informational materials on China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a letter from Ina Bowers requesting informational materials and maps on China and Japan.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet regarding Inquiry by Miss Ina Bowers on China and Japan

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet and political report excerpt analyzing quiet Diet proceedings in February 1933 and rumors of cabinet changes involving Dr. Kisaburo Suzuki.
subfiles.summary: Despatch excerpt on February 1933 Japanese politics: subdued Diet sessions, rumors the Saito Cabinet might fall, speculation Finance Minister Takahashi could yield to Yamamoto, and Suzuki might take the Home Ministry ahead of elections.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet with Extract from Despatch No. 288 on February Political Developments in Japan

subfiles.about: A State Department file charge slip noting the withdrawal or transfer of documents 894.00/473 and 894.00/474.
subfiles.summary: Charge slip documents checkout of files 894.00/473 and /474, noting transfers involving Peiping and other handling.
subfiles.title: Charge Slip for Files 894.00/473 and 894.00/474

subfiles.about: A State Department cross-reference note recording Despatch No. 2003 from Peiping enclosing T.V. Soong's statement and newspaper editorials on Chinese warlordism.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Johnson's despatch enclosing T.V. Soong's statement condemning warlordism and related Peiping/Tientsin editorials, tied to the Manchurian conflict.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet regarding Despatch No. 2003 on T.V. Soong's Statements on Warlordism

subfiles.about: Minister Johnson reports on former Japanese Foreign Minister Yoshizawa's visit to Peiping, Chinese refusal to negotiate, and Yoshizawa's anticipation of a Seiyukai cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Johnson reports Yoshizawa's Peiping visit failed to secure talks with Chinese leaders after Japan's Jehol invasion; Yoshizawa expected Tokyo's cabinet to fall by mid-1933, with himself as the Seiyukai's Foreign Minister.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet and Telegram No. 330 on Kenkichi Yoshizawa's Visit to Peiping

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew assesses rumors of the Saito Cabinet's imminent fall, citing Prince Saionji's desire for stability and moderate Japanese hopes for eventual conciliation.
subfiles.summary: Grew tells Johnson reports of the Saito Cabinet's imminent collapse are premature, since Prince Saionji wants it to remain until Japan's diplomatic isolation eases, with moderates hoping a successor cabinet turns conciliatory.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet and Telegram No. 80 on Japanese Cabinet Prospects and Foreign Policy Reorientation
